title: Kitchen Chemistry
summary: How cooking shows the difference between physical changes, like melting and dissolving, and chemical changes, like cooking an egg, rising dough, and roasting coffee beans.
poll: A kitchen is a good place to learn science.

versions.title: Science in the Kitchen
versions.text:
Your kitchen is like a lab. Cooks use chemistry each day. Chemistry is the study of stuff. It is how stuff can change.

Some changes are small. Ice melts in the sun. It turns to water. Put the water in the cold. It is ice once more. Butter can melt, too. This kind of change can go back.

Put sugar in hot tea. Stir it. The sugar dissolves. You can not see it. But the tea is sweet. So the sugar is still there.

Some changes make new stuff. They can not go back. Cook an egg. The clear part turns white. It gets firm. It can not be raw once more. Toast bread. It turns brown. It smells good.

Mix a bit of baking soda with vinegar. It fizzes! The bubbles are a gas. Gas helps cake rise. In bread dough, yeast makes the gas. The dough gets big and soft.

In Saudi Arabia, green coffee beans are roasted. Heat turns them brown. They get a new smell.

Look for signs of new stuff. Look for bubbles. Look for a new hue or smell. Cook with a grown-up near you. Heat can burn. Be safe.

versions.title: Kitchen Chemistry
versions.text:
Your kitchen is a lot like a science lab. Every time someone cooks a meal, they are doing chemistry. Chemistry is the study of what substances are made of and how they change.

Some changes are physical changes. A physical change alters the shape or form of a substance, but it does not make a new one. When ice melts in the sun, it turns into liquid water. If you put that water in the freezer, it freezes into ice again. Butter melts in a hot pan and gets solid again in the fridge.

Dissolving is also a physical change. When you stir sugar into hot tea, the sugar seems to disappear. But the tea tastes sweet, so the sugar is still there. If all the water dried up, the sugar would be left behind.

Other changes are chemical changes. In a chemical change, a new substance forms, and it usually cannot be turned back. When you cook an egg, the clear part turns white and firm. It can never be raw again. When bread is toasted, its surface turns brown and smells great.

A chemical change is also called a reaction. Mix baking soda with vinegar, and the reaction makes bubbles of a gas called carbon dioxide. In a cake, these bubbles help the batter rise. In bread dough, tiny living things called yeast make the same gas, so the dough puffs up.

In Saudi Arabia, people roast green coffee beans for Arabic coffee. The heat causes a reaction that turns the beans brown and makes a rich new smell.

Scientists look for clues of a chemical change: bubbles, a new color, a new smell, or heat. Always cook with an adult nearby, because hot pans can burn.

versions.title: Kitchen Chemistry: Changes You Can Eat
versions.text:
Your kitchen is remarkably similar to a science laboratory, because every time someone prepares a meal, they are practicing chemistry, the scientific study of what substances are composed of and how they transform under different conditions, often without the cook ever realizing it.

Some kitchen changes are physical changes, which alter the shape, size, or state of a substance without producing an additional substance, so they can usually be reversed. When ice melts in the sunshine, it becomes liquid water, and if that water returns to the freezer, it solidifies into ice once again; similarly, butter liquefies in a heated pan and becomes solid again when it cools in the refrigerator. Such transformations rearrange a substance's outward appearance while leaving its fundamental identity completely unchanged.

Dissolving is another physical change. When you stir sugar into hot tea, the sugar appears to vanish completely; however, the tea tastes noticeably sweet, which demonstrates that the sugar is still present, distributed evenly among the water molecules, and if all the water evaporated, the sugar crystals would remain behind in the cup, proving that nothing was genuinely lost in the process.

Other changes are chemical changes, in which an entirely new substance forms and the transformation is usually irreversible. When an egg is cooked, heat permanently rearranges the protein in the transparent egg white, which consequently becomes opaque and firm and can never become raw again, regardless of how carefully it is subsequently cooled. When bread is toasted, its surface turns brown and develops a delicious, complicated aroma that untoasted bread does not possess, because entirely new flavor compounds have formed within it.

A chemical change is also called a reaction. Baking soda is a base and vinegar is an acid, so when the two are combined, the reaction immediately produces bubbles of a gas called carbon dioxide. In a cake, these bubbles become trapped in the batter and allow it to rise, while in bread dough, microscopic organisms called yeast generate the identical gas as they gradually consume sugar, so the dough steadily expands over several hours of resting.

In Saudi Arabia, families roast green coffee beans to prepare traditional Arabic coffee, and the intense heat triggers numerous simultaneous reactions that transform the beans to brown and generate a rich, unfamiliar aroma that no raw, unroasted bean could ever produce on its own.

Scientists look for evidence that a chemical change has occurred, including bubbles, an unexpected color, a distinctive new odor, or released energy, any one of which signals that the original substance has been permanently transformed into something new. Always cook with an adult nearby, because heated pans and ovens can cause serious, painful injuries that require immediate medical attention, and because recognizing these changes safely is part of learning real kitchen chemistry.

versions.title: Kitchen Chemistry: Changes You Can Eat
versions.text:
Your ordinary household kitchen bears a remarkable and somewhat underappreciated resemblance to an actual scientific research laboratory, because every single time someone prepares even a simple meal, they are inadvertently practicing fundamental chemistry, the rigorous scientific discipline specifically concerned with precisely what substances are fundamentally composed of at a molecular level and precisely how those substances transform under systematically varying environmental conditions.

Certain routine kitchen transformations qualify technically as physical changes, which alter merely the external shape, size, or physical state of a given substance without producing any genuinely additional new substance in the process, meaning they can usually be readily and completely reversed under appropriate conditions. When solid ice melts gradually under warm ambient sunshine, it transforms directly into liquid water, and if that same water subsequently returns to a sufficiently cold freezer, it solidifies back into ice once again; similarly, solid butter liquefies readily within a heated cooking pan and subsequently becomes solid once more as soon as it cools sufficiently within a refrigerator.

Dissolving represents another characteristic and frequently observed physical change. When you stir granulated sugar thoroughly into hot tea, the sugar crystals appear to vanish completely from visual observation; however, the resulting tea nevertheless tastes noticeably and persistently sweet, which conclusively demonstrates that the sugar remains genuinely present throughout, distributed evenly at a molecular level throughout the surrounding water molecules, and if all that water subsequently evaporated entirely away, the original sugar crystals would predictably remain behind within the empty cup.

Other kitchen transformations qualify instead as genuine chemical changes, in which an entirely new chemical substance forms and the resulting transformation typically proves permanently irreversible under ordinary conditions. When a raw egg undergoes cooking, applied thermal heat permanently and irreversibly rearranges the protein structure within the previously transparent egg white, which consequently becomes visibly opaque and firm in texture and can categorically never subsequently become raw again, regardless of how carefully or thoroughly it is subsequently cooled afterward. When ordinary bread undergoes toasting, its exposed surface turns noticeably and progressively brown in color and develops a genuinely delicious, chemically complicated aroma that untoasted bread categorically does not possess under any circumstances.

A chemical change of this kind is also formally and technically termed a reaction. Ordinary baking soda functions chemically as what scientists call a base, while vinegar functions chemically as what scientists call an acid, so whenever these two substances are deliberately combined together, the resulting chemical reaction immediately produces visible bubbles of a specific gas formally called carbon dioxide. Within a baking cake, these generated gas bubbles become physically trapped throughout the surrounding batter and consequently allow the entire cake to rise properly during baking, while within fermenting bread dough, microscopic living single-celled organisms called yeast generate that identical gas as they gradually and continuously consume available sugar molecules, causing the dough to steadily and visibly expand in overall volume.

In Saudi Arabia specifically, families traditionally and ceremonially roast green, unroasted coffee beans to prepare authentic traditional Arabic coffee, and the intensely applied heat triggers numerous simultaneous and interconnected chemical reactions that progressively transform the beans from green to brown while simultaneously generating a rich, distinctively unfamiliar, and highly characteristic aroma.

Scientists characteristically and systematically look for specific observable evidence that a genuine chemical change has actually occurred, including visible gas bubbles, an unexpected color transformation, a distinctive new odor, or measurably released thermal energy. Always cook exclusively alongside a supervising, responsible adult present nearby, because heated pans and ovens can potentially and unpredictably cause serious, genuinely painful injuries that require immediate professional medical attention.

keyWords.definition: the science of what things are made of and how they change
keyWords.example: In chemistry class, we mixed two liquids and watched the color change.

keyWords.definition: to turn from a solid into a liquid because of heat
keyWords.example: My ice cream began to melt in the hot car.

keyWords.definition: to mix into a liquid so you can no longer see it
keyWords.example: Salt will dissolve if you stir it into warm water.

keyWords.definition: a form of matter, like air, that spreads out and has no shape
keyWords.example: The balloon floated because it was filled with a light gas.

keyWords.definition: a soft mix of flour and water used to make bread

How cooking shows that things can change in different ways

wrong.C: The article talks about roasting coffee beans, not growing them.

MID.prompt: Explain the difference between a physical change and a chemical change. Use one kitchen example of each from the article.

MID.modelAnswer: A physical change does not make a new substance; it just changes the shape or form, like when ice melts into liquid water and could freeze back again. A chemical change is a reaction that makes a brand new substance that usually cannot go back, like when baking soda and vinegar react and make bubbles of carbon dioxide gas.

HIGH.prompt: Choose two examples from the article, one physical change and one chemical change. Explain the evidence that tells you which kind of change each one is.
checklist: I described one physical change and why it can be reversed.
I described one chemical change and the new substance or clue it shows.
I used details such as bubbles, color, smell, or protein from the article.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Melting butter in a hot pan is a physical change, since it is reversible: the butter turns solid again once it cools in the fridge, with no new substance formed. Cooking an egg, however, is an irreversible chemical change, because the heat changes the protein in the egg white so it turns from clear to firm and white, and it can never return to its raw form. The clue that tells them apart is reversibility: one change can undo itself, while the other permanently transforms the molecules involved.
